A B S T R A C T

Fall-from-height (FFH) accidents remain a leading cause of fatalities in the construction industry. To systemat ically extract and analyze risk factors from unstructured FFH accident reports. this paper emploved large lan: guage models (LLMs) to enable zero-shot automated fall-from-height knowledge graph (FFHKG) construction. By clustering FFHKG entities to merge semantically similar factors, a weighted complex network is formed. enabling topological analysis for quantitative risk assessment. A case study on 1097 FFH accident reports validates the proposed framework. Results demonstrate that GPT-4o achieves high extraction accuracy, with an F1 score of 0.94 in named entity recognition and a precision of 0.90 in relationship extraction. Key risk factors, such as poor safety management, lack of training, insufficient edge protection, etc., are quantitatively identified across multiple perspectives. Observable unsafe behaviors are also detected, offering insights for behavior-based safety monitoring. The proposed framework provides a data-driven solution for more effective safety management on construction sites.
1. Introduction

The construction sector serves as a fundamental component of the national economy. Nevertheless, the combination of mechanized oper ations, manual labor, and the inherently complex and ever-changing work environment poses persistent safety challenges. Among all acci dent types in this field, fall-from-height (FFH) accidents remain the primary cause of fatalities, contributing to roughly 40 % of constructionrelated deaths [1]. For example, in 2020, there were 4764 recorded fatalities in the U.S. construction industry [2], while the UK reported 39 fatal cases (equivalent to a rate of 1.62 deaths per 100,000 workers), markedly higher than the 0.65 per 100,000 observed in the manufacturing sector [3]. Although advancements in safety manage ment have led to a gradual decline in FFH-related fatalities, these acci dents remain a pressing concern worldwide. Effectively reducing FFH accidents requires a thorough understanding of their underlying risk factors and accurate risk assessment methods to support decision making in construction safety management.

To evaluate FFH risk factors, researchers have traditionally relied on expert knowledge to construct expert-based systems that quantify the importance of various factors [4,5]. However, expert judgment is inherently subjective, and obtaining reliable and extensive expert rat ings remains challenging [6]. The construction industry has accumu lated a vast number of accident reports that are now readily accessible online. Leveraging historical accident data offers a more objective approach to identifying risk factors and trends, reducing the potential bias introduced by expert assessments [7]. Existing data-driven methods for accident analysis can be broadly classified into two categories. The first approach involves statistical analysis of structured accident data, where researchers extract patterns related to accident frequency, severity, and distribution [8,9]. While this method effectively uncovers historical trends, it struggles to capture complex causal interactions among risk factors. Construction accidents often result from a chain reaction of multiple hazards rather than isolated causes. To address these limitations, researchers have introduced System Accident Analysis (SAA) models to analyze accident mechanisms [10]. Classical models such as the Domino Model, Swiss Cheese Model, Accident Mapping (AcciMap). System-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP). and Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) attempt to repre sent accident causality [11]. These models offer valuable insights into how risk factors interact and escalate into accidents. However, they primarily serve as conceptual frameworks and lack the capability to perform quantitative analysis, making it difficult to accurately measure the degree of influence among risk factors.

Network theory provides an effective means of quantitatively analyzing and visualizing complex causal relationships [12]. Among various network-based approaches, knowledge graph (KG) has emerged as a powerful tool for capturing and representing structured knowledge [13]. By abstracting interrelated entities as connected nodes and defining their relationships, KG has been widely applied in knowledge modeling and risk analysis across multiple domains [14,15]. In the context of construction safety, KG offers a promising approach for the multi-dimensional modeling of accident causality. However, a major challenge in KG construction for construction safety lies in the un structured nature of accident reports. Existing approaches often rely on manual annotation and coding, which is labor-intensive, timeconsuming, and impractical, given the increasing volume of accident records [16]. The emergence of Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques has enabled automated knowledge extraction from unstruc tured text, paving the way for KG automation. Some studies have trained information extraction models using manually annotated datasets [17]. However, the construction safety domain lacks large-scale, well-anno tated corpora, limiting the generalization ability of such models.

With the rapid advancement of NLP, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in processing and under standing human language, significantly enhancing the efficiency of in formation extraction [18]. LLMs offer a scalable solution for analyzing vast amounts of unstructured accident reports, enabling the automated construction of KG without relying on extensive labeled datasets. A promising technique in this domain is prompt engineering, which op timizes LLM output for downstream tasks without requiring model retraining [19]. By formulating structured prompts, researchers can guide LLMs to extract relevant causal relationships from accident reports flexibly and resource-efficiently. This approach reduces the dependence on large, annotated datasets while maintaining adaptability across different accident scenarios. Given the increasing complexity of risk factor interactions in FFH accidents, leveraging LLMs for automated KG construction offers a powerful tool for advancing data-driven accident analysis.

This paper aims to leverage LLMs to construct fall-from-height knowledge graphs (FFHKG) from unstructured accident reports to quantitatively analyze risk factors in FFH accidents. The main research questions in this paper are: (1) How can structured knowledge be accurately extracted from unstructured accident reports under a zeroshot learning paradigm to construct a reliable FFHKG? (2) How can the FFHKG be used to quantitatively analyze causal relationships and identify key risk factors for FFH accidents? To solve these questions, this paper first constructs the FFHKG automatically using LLMs. The entities within the FFHKG are subsequently semantically embedded and grouped using hierarchical clustering, enabling the fusion of similar entities and the transformation of the FFHKG into a weighted complex network that is easier to analyze. Topological analysis is then applied to quantify the influence of each risk factor from different perspectives. The novelty of this research lies in (a) developing a KG structure inte grated with the AcciMap model, enabling a comprehensive representa tion of multi-level causality in FFH accidents; (b) constructing a promptbased information extraction pipeline that enables zero-shot, LLMpowered KG construction without the need for annotated training data; (c) conducting a systematic and objective quantitative analysis of risk factors through the networked causal structure extracted from a large corpus of real-world accident reports.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 comprehensively reviews existing studies on FFH accident factors analysis and automated KG construction. Section 3 details the proposed methodology. Section 4 reports the results of a case study of 1097 FFH accidents, while Section 5 provides further discussion. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines limitations and directions for future research.
2. Related studies

Understanding the underlying causes of FFH accidents and effec tively structuring the associated knowledge are both critical for improving construction safety. Therefore, this section reviews existing studies on FFH risk factor analysis and the automated construction of knowledge graph from unstructured accident data.
2.1. Risk factors analysis of fall-from-height accident

Numerous studies have investigated the risk factors associated with FFH accidents. Based on the existing literature, these factors can be broadly categorized into four groups: organizational and management factors, equipment-related factors, environmental factors, and individ ual factors. Organizational and management risks include insufficient safety training, poor management practices, and inadequate safety su pervision. For example, Luo et al. [20] utilized the Apriori algorithm to examine 557 FFH accidents reported on construction sites from 2013 to 2019 and identified insufficient safety training and site complexity as major contributing factors. Similarly, Nawi et al. [21] used question naire data analyzed through a Likert scale and reported that inadequate education and poor management were primary contributors to FFH accidents. Equipment-related factors mainly include the absence or improper use of personal protective equipment (PPE). Kang [22] con ducted frequency analysis alongside chi-square and Kruskal–Wallis tests on FFH accident data from 1997 to 2012, revealing that more than 70 % of these accidents were linked to the absence of fall protection equip ment. Cheng et al. [23] used data mining methods to investigate construction-related occupational accidents in Taiwan and found that the most commonly reported contributors to FFH accidents included improper or missing PPE, insufficient safety awareness, and neglect of hazard warnings. Environmental factors also play a crucial role in FFH accidents. These include complex site layouts, adverse weather condi tions. and deficiencies in safety installations such as guardrails and scaffolding. Bobick [24] examined the Bureau of Labor Statistics from 1992 to 2000 and identified the absence of guardrails as a leading contributor to FFH accidents. Halperin et al. [25] evaluated scaffold safety at nine construction sites using a standardized checklist. highlighting missing planks, inadequate guardrails, and poor access as sig nificant hazards. Individual factors primarily involve workers’ behavior, experience, and risk perception. Wong et al. [26] reported that poor safety attitudes and behaviors among workers posed major challenges to construction site safety management. Jahangiri et al. [27] also found that improper use of PPE and workers' neglect of protective measures were common risk behaviors. In a study focused on the Malaysiar construction sector, Ayob et al. [28] reported that 46.28 % of FFH ac cidents were linked to safety regulation violations, inadequate use of PPE, unsafe practices, and ineffective management.

However, FFH risk factors do not exist in isolation but are interre lated and mutually influential. For instance, poor management can lead to the absence of safety equipment, thereby increasing the risk of acci dents; similarly, unfavorable site conditions may exacerbate unsafe in dividual behavior. Although previous studies have identified various risk factors, limited attention has been paid to the interactions among them. Traditional statistical methods are insufficient to capture the dy namic interplay between multiple contributing factors. To overcome the limitations of traditional statistical approaches, some studies have adopted SAA models to examine the interdependence among various factors and uncover the underlying mechanisms of accidents in complex construction site environments. The Human Factors Analysis and Clas sification System (HFACS) framework categorizes accident causes into four hierarchical levels: unsafe acts, preconditions for unsafe acts, un safe supervision, and organizational influences [29]. Qi et al. [30] an notated data using a modified HFACS framework and automatically extracted risk factors from FFH accident reports, ultimately identifying 19 risk factors across the four categories. However, their application in the FFH safety domain remains limited. In the broader context of con struction site safety, Ma et al. While SAA models provide a structured framework to capture the hierarchical and interactive nature of FFH accident causation, most existing studies emphasize qualitative classification rather than quan titative analysis of the relationships among factors. This shortcoming hinders the identification of critical risks and the prioritization of pre ventive interventions. To address this gap, complex network theory presents a promising approach by modeling risk factors as nodes and their interactions as edges. This enables the application of network metrics (e.g., centrality, clustering coefficient) to evaluate the impor tance and connectivity of risk factors [33]. Given that KG inherently possesses a network structure, it offers an ideal platform to integrate SAA-based classifications with quantitative causal inference. Although complex network theory has been successfully applied in accident analysis in other domains [12,33], it has not yet been widely imple mented in the context of FFH risk analysis. Therefore, this paper pro poses a method for constructing an automated FFHKG grounded in the AcciMap model. By applying network analysis techniques to FFHKG, we aim to quantify the strength of causal relationships among risk factors, thereby providing a scalable, data-driven framework for comprehensive FFH risk assessment.
2.2. Automated knowledge graph construction

Building a comprehensive and efficient KG requires accurate infor mation extraction to transform unstructured text into structured repre sentations. However, accident reports are typically lengthy, unstructured, and contain complex causal relationships, making high precision and high-efficiency KG construction particularly challenging. Some studies rely on manual extraction due to limited data availability, but this approach is time-consuming, costly, and highly dependent on subjective interpretation. As accident records grow, manual methods become impractical for large-scale knowledge extraction.

To address these challenges, NLP techniques have been employed for automated KG construction. Traditional KG construction involves named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (RE) [34]. Gan et al. [35] utilized NLP to extract textual information from maritime accident reports, enabling structured KG queries to reveal accident patterns. Wang et al. [36] tested convolutional neural network and recurrent neural network models for relation extraction in construction safety regulations, achieving an accuracy of 87.5 %. Chen et al. [13] proposed a novel model based on a pre-trained language model for water conservancy safety management, reaching over 85 % accuracy in text recognition. While these studies demonstrate the potential of NLp for KG construction, their effectiveness is highly dependent on large, well-annotated datasets. These models perform well on training data but often fail to generalize across different document formats and domains. Moreover, accident reports vary in structure, covering diverse entities related to people, behaviors, environments, and organizations. Unlike general NLP tasks (e.g., extracting names and locations), KG construc tion for accident analysis requires not only “recognition” but also deep “understanding” of text content.

Given the limitations of traditional NLP models, LLMs offer a promising alternative for KG construction. LLMs generate diverse out puts based on prompts, making them highly adaptable for information extraction tasks. Wei et al. [37] demonstrated that state-of-the-art LLMs exhibit excellent zero-shot and few-shot extraction capabilities, reducing dependence on large annotated datasets. Ashok et al. [38] introduced Prompt-NER, which enhances entity recognition by prompting LLMs to generate comprehensive lists of potential entities. In a systematic evaluation, Li et al. [39] assessed GPT-3.5’s performance in open information extraction but noted its limitations in handling com plex relationship extraction tasks. Trajanoska et al. [40] proposed an LLM-enhanced KG pipeline that integrates entity and relation extraction, demonstrating improved performance in domain-specific knowledge structuring. These findings suggest that LLMs can enhance KG con struction efficiency and accuracy for accident analysis.

Despite LLMs’ potential, their application in the construction in dustry remains at an early stage, particularly for unstructured accident report analysis. Researchers have yet to systematically evaluate LLMs performance in extracting construction-specific knowledge from un structured texts. Current studies lack a comparative analysis of different LLM architectures for accident-related IE tasks. Therefore, this paper aims to develop an LLM-based prompt engineering approach to effi ciently process large-scale unstructured accident reports, transforming them into structured FFHKG components for comprehensive risk assessment.
3. Methodology

This study develops an LLM-based framework for automated FFHKG construction and quantitative analysis of risk factors from unstructured accident reports. The overall workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1. First, the KG ontology is established by adjusting the classical AcciMap model to capture the hierarchical and causal structure of construction FFH acci dents. Then, a prompt engineering strategy is introduced, combining Prompt Chaining, Chain of Thought reasoning, and Self-Consistency sampling to enable zero-shot information extraction for FFHKG gener ation using LLMs. The entities of FFHKG are embedded into dense vec tors and clustered using hierarchical agglomerative clustering to fuse semantically similar nodes. The FFHKG is then transformed into a weighted complex network that is more suitable for structural analysis. Finally, topological analysis is applied to quantify the influence of each factor from three perspectives: direct causality, indirect causality, and accident risk propagation, providing a comprehensive understanding of the key contributors to FFH accidents.
3.1. Construction of FFHKG ontology

KG is a structured representation of knowledge in the form of a se mantic network, where entities, concepts, and events are linked through meaningful relationships [41]. By embedding semantic metadata into these connections, KG enables data integration, contextual under standing, and advanced reasoning across heterogeneous sources. Ontology provides the formal semantic foundation of KG, defining the types of entities, their attributes, and relationships. As the schema of the graph, ontology ensures consistent interpretation and semantic inter operability across domains.

In the domain of construction safety, KGs offer a promising tool to systematically capture complex causality of accidents. Accident reports often contain detailed but unstructured descriptions of unsafe behaviors, faulty equipment, and organizational failures. To support automated knowledge extraction and causal reasoning in this context, a domain specific ontology is needed to represent the hierarchical structure and interactions among multiple facilities, personnel, and management layers. To achieve this, the AcciMap framework is adopted as the foundation for constructing the FFHKG ontology. Originally proposed by Rasmussen, AcciMap is designed to identify failures, decisions, and ac tions across different levels of a socio-technical system and to analyze the interactions among these elements that lead to accidents [42]. As illustrated in Fig. 2(a), the original AcciMap framework comprises six hierarchical levels aligned with risk management structures. This hier archical structure allows both bottom-up classification and top-down causality tracing, making it well-suited for modeling accident causation in construction sites [43].

To address this limitation, this study modified AcciMap to better suit construction site accident analysis, as shown in Fig. 2(b). Construction sites have a well-established safety supervision system where Owners, Supervisors, Contractors, and Subcontractors operate under contractua and supervisory relationships. Given that these relationships signifi cantly impact safety management, the original AcciMap framework’s first four levels have been adjusted to reflect the hierarchical structure of construction projects. The “Government” and “Association” levels in the original framework have been replaced by “Owner” and “Supervisor” to reflect the directly involved entities in construction safety supervision. Additionally, to improve the representation of accident causation, in dependent “Equipment” and “Surroundings” categories have been introduced as intermediaries between management layers and individ ual activities. Accidents are influenced not only by worker behavior but also by equipment conditions and environmental factors. Thus, the original fifth level has been divided into Individual Activities and Ac cident Processes, where worker actions influence accident progression, affecting subsequent behavior. The revised AcciMap framework en hances clarity and consistency in representing causal relationships specific to FFH accidents.

Based on the modified AcciMap framework, this study constructs the FFHKG ontology, as shown in Fig. 3. The ontology consists of eight entity categories corresponding to the adjusted AcciMap levels: Owner, Supervisor, Contractor, Subcontractor, Equipment, Surroundings, Indi vidual activities, and Accident status. In addition to these primary knowledge entities, project-related attributes, such as project type, ac cident date, location, and consequences, are incorporated to enrich the contextual representation of accidents. A complete list of the knowledge entity types is shown in Table 1.

The relationships between entities are determined based on thei type, with six predefined relationship categories. To reflect the multilayered causality structure of FFH accidents, the ontology defines three types of causal relationships: “Cause”, “Trigger”, and “Lead\_to” [7,14]. Each corresponds to a different stage in the accident formation process. Specifically, “Cause” captures indirect and organizational-level causes; “Trigger” represents direct and immediate causes; and “Lead\_to” links the sequential events during the accident itself. By differentiating these stages, the knowledge graph can represent not only who or what contributed to the accident but also how risk factors evolved over time, supporting both root cause tracing and scenario reconstruction. This structure also aligns with layered safety models such as AcciMap, where system-level and individual-level influences are disentangled across time and responsibility dimensions. In addition, two hierarchical re lationships are defined: “Value\_is” and “Type\_is” [44,45]. “Value\_is” links entities to quantitative attributes. “Type\_is” associates entities with qualitative attributes. This ontology provides a structured and scalable foundation for automated knowledge extraction and risk factor analysis

3.2. LLM-driven automated generation of FFHKG

NLP serves as the foundation for automatically constructing KG by extracting structured knowledge triples < e , r, e >, where e and e are entities, and r represents their relationship. With the emergence of LLMs, NLP has unlocked new possibilities for zero-shot information extraction. This section introduces the approach used to construct prompts for LLMs to enable zero-shot extraction of knowledge triples, followed by methods for evaluating extraction quality and constructing and visualizing the resulting FFHKG.

While LLMs have shown the potential to extract complete triples in a single pass directly, their short internal reasoning chains often lead to hallucinated outputs and unstable performance in complex inference tasks. To improve the extraction accuracy of LLMs, this study de composes the triple extraction task into two classic NLP sub-processes: NER and RE. Then, they are connected through chained prompts (CP),
3.2.1. Identification of knowledge entities

NER refers to identifying and classifying words or phrases in text into predefined entity categories. In this study, the information extraction process begins with detecting relevant entities from accident reports. To fully leverage LLMs for the NER task, the prompts are designed based on the following four principles: (1) clear role assignment, (2) contextual learning, (3) Chain of Thought reasoning, and (4) structured output formatting. The complete prompt structure is illustrated in Fig. 4.

First, the LLM is assigned the role of a “construction safety expert.” Then, the relevant accident text is provided, and the model is prompted to extract entities based on its contextual understanding. To enhance the reasoning process, Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning is applied to guide the model through step-by-step logical inference, enabling more accu rate and explainable outputs. Since different entity types play distinct roles in accident causation, we designed separate prompt tasks tailored to each entity category. Entities are grouped into three categories. Task A targets management-related entities (e.g., Own, Sup, Con, and Sub), which are typically associated with indirect causes of accidents. Task B focuses on physical context entities, including Equ and Surr, which usually represent direct causes of accidents. Task C captures the timeline chain of the accident by linking Individual Activity with Accident Status. The remaining entity types are basic information and can be extracted through direct queries without requiring CoT reasoning. Finally, the extracted entities are standardized and output in JSON format. This structured output facilitates seamless integration with Python dictio naries, supporting downstream tasks such as relationship extraction between entities.
3.2.2. Extraction of knowledge relation

RE aims to identify relationships between entity pairs in text, essentially classifying the potential relationships between entities. In this study, entity relationships are inferred by prompting LLMs to analyze detailed accident report content. Some relationships, such as “Value\_is”, “Type\_is”, and “Lead\_to”, can be directly determined without complex reasoning. This is because each accident report typically con tains only one specific attribute for such fields (e.g., a single economic loss value per accident), making hierarchical relationships like “Val ue\_is” and “Type\_is” easily identifiable based on the entity type. Addi tionally, the “Lead\_to” relationship, which connects Individual Activity and Accident Status, can be directly derived from the timeline structure obtained in the previous step. However, the causal relationships of “Cause” and “Trigger” require more intricate reasoning.

3.2.3. Evaluation of extraction performance

Assessing the accuracy of entities and relationships extracted by LLMs is essential to ensure the reliability and practical value of the FFHKG. Human expertise plays a crucial role in evaluating the quality and correctness of the extracted information and in identifying relevant entities that may have been missed. Therefore, manual annotation by domain experts is employed as the reference standard. For entity eval uation, experts first determine whether the extracted entity is mentioned in the report and whether its type is correctly identified. They also annotate any relevant entities present in the report that were not extracted by the model. For relationships, experts assess whether the linked entities are accurate and whether the relation is appropriately expressed in the report. To minimize subjective bias, multiple experts independently evaluate each extraction. Inter-annotator agreement is quantified using Fleiss’ Kappa, which statistically measures the consis tency among annotators and ensures the reliability of the reference standard [46]. Only the annotations that meet the agreement threshold are used as the final reference standard for subsequent performance evaluation.

This study employs well-known metrics to assess the quality of the extracted entities and relationships. The extraction quality of both en tities and entity relationships will be evaluated separately. We first use the classic confusion matrix entries to evaluate the performance of extracting each component. Specifically, correctly extracted components are considered True Positives (TP), while incorrect ones are labeled as False Positives (FP), and missing entities are treated as False Negatives (FN). Based on these classifications, Precision (P) is computed as the ratio of correct results to all retrieved results, and Recall (R) is the ratio of correct results to all relevant results. The F1 score, defined as the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, provides a balanced evaluation of both metrics.

3.3. Knowledge fusion of FFHKG

Accident reports are unstructured texts, and the expressions of various entities may be inconsistent. For instance, entities such as “insufficient safety training,” “lack of full-time safety training,” and “no safety training provided” all refer to the same concept of “insufficient safety training” but are expressed differently. Displaying all entities with the same meaning would significantly increase the complexity of the network. Therefore, it is necessary to fuse knowledge by merging mul tiple entities with the same meaning into a single entity. In this section, we first use pre-trained models for entity embedding, then apply unsu pervised hierarchical clustering to return subsets of semantically similar entities or relationships, thus integrating the KG into a more under standable weighted complex network structure. Since the complex network is designed for quantitative analysis of influencing factors, basic information entities are excluded from the clustering process.
3.3.1. Knowledge embedding

Knowledge embedding involves transforming textual information into vectorized numerical forms that preserve semantic relationships among words, sentences, or entire documents [47]. Based on textual granularity, embedding techniques are typically classified into wordlevel, sentence-level, and document-level embeddings. Since the knowledge entities obtained in the previous section are in the form of phrases, this study selects sentence-level embedding using pre-trained models, which map the entire phrase into fixed-length vectors.

However, sentence vectors generated by transformer-based models such as BERT are often constrained to a small region in the vector space and tend to exhibit excessive similarity, which limits their effectiveness in distinguishing semantically different entities. To address this issue, the Cosine Sentence (CoSENT) method was proposed to improve sen tence representation by better aligning it with the data distributions of downstream tasks [48]. Based on CoSENT, a “shibing624/text2vec-basechinese-paraphrase” model is trained, incorporating a contrastive loss function that maximizes the similarity of positive sentence pairs while minimizing the similarity of negative pairs [49], as defined in Eq. 3.3.2. Knowledge clustering

After vectorizing the entities using pre-trained models, similar en tities need to be aggregated through clustering. A common method for clustering is by the comparing cosine similarity between vectors. How ever, text similarity is more suitable for pairwise comparison and does not directly apply to generating different groupings. Clustering algo rithms, a category of unsupervised learning techniques, divide datasets into groups of instances sharing similar characteristics. Common ap proaches include hierarchical clustering, K-means, and DBSCAN. In this study, however, the optimal number of clusters for each entity type is unknown, and cluster centroids cannot be predefined. Therefore, we use Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC) to eliminate the need for initial group center selection and enhance the stability of the clustering results. HAC is a bottom-up single-linkage hierarchical clustering method [50]. It offers advantages in complex clustering scenarios, as it does not require predefining the number of clusters or initializing cen troids and is less prone to local optima.

HAC starts by considering each data point as a separate cluster and iteratively merges the pair of clusters with the highest similarity until a specified stopping condition is reached. After the clustering process is complete, hierarchical results at any level can be obtained, providing extensive data to evaluate the similarity between factors, as shown in Fig. 7. During clustering, the feature vector sequence of entities is denoted as $F = \{ f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \cdots , f _ { N } \}$ , where N denotes the total number of en tities. These vectors are partitioned by a set of segment boundaries $T =$ $\{ t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , \cdots , t _ { S } \}$ , where S denotes the total number of segments. The objective of HAC is to determine the optimal boundary set that mini mizes the within-cluster square error function $f ( F , T ) ,$ as defined in Eq. (7). The number of segments S corresponds to the final number of clusters L when $f ( F , T )$ reaches its minimum value. HAC allows for data driven segmentation of entities to balance over-segmentation and undersegmentation without requiring manually predefined cluster numbers.

After aggregating semantically similar entities through hierarchical clustering, each cluster is assigned a representative category name, referred to as a risk factor. The final step involves mapping these clus tered risk factors and their weighted causal links onto a weighted complex network. The weighted complex network is represented by the weighted adjacency matrix AM<sup>w</sup>, defined by Eq. (8).

4. Case study

To validate the effectiveness and applicability of the proposed methodology, this section presents a case study based on real-world FFH accident data. A large-scale dataset of construction site FFH accident reports was collected and analyzed. The FFHKG was automatically constructed using LLMs and subsequently refined into a complex network to enable quantitative analysis of risk factors.
4.1. Data collection

To construct the database for construction site FFH accidents. this study collected a total of 4590 accident cases using web crawlers. The detailed accident reports were obtained from the “Safety Production Management” section on the official websites of various provincial and municipal governments in China. Additionally, using search engines on government websites, keywords such as “fall-from-height accidents,” “accident reports,” and “accident investigations” were employed to search for accident cases directly. After thorough filtering, 1097 acci dent cases were retained for the dataset in this study. The filtering process followed two main principles: (1) Only accidents with detailed reports, including direct and indirect causes, were retained. Many cases were recorded on websites with minimal information, making it difficult to extract risk factors. These cases were excluded from the dataset. (2) Only accidents in the past ten years were selected. Earlier data may not accurately reflect the current state of safety management on construc tion sites, as it may lack recent updates and safety practices. Therefore, accidents from 2014 to 2023 were chosen. Additionally, many accident reports are removed from government websites after some time, so the reports collected in this study represent all available reports from 2014 to 2023. While the 1097 cases are not the total number of FFH accidents in China during this period, they contain detailed information useful for further analysis. All reports were converted into .txt format for unifor mity in data processing.
4.2. FHHKG construction and fusion

Building on the collected accident report dataset, this section demonstrates the practical implementation of FFHKG construction and fusion. It presents the LLM-based extraction results and subsequent knowledge fusion process, which collectively support the development of a complex network for risk analysis.

4.2.1. Extraction results of FFHKG

Different LLMs exhibit varying performance in causal reasoning, long-text comprehension, and computational efficiency. 5. Discussion

To further examine the effectiveness of the proposed methodology and its relevance to practical construction safety improvement, this section presents additional experimental validation and corresponding risk mitigation insights.
5.1. Ablation experiment

This study introduces an LLM-powered approach for extracting causal knowledge from accident reports without labeled data as a novel methodological attempt, achieving promising results. To verify the effectiveness of each component in our proposed prompt engineering, we conducted ablation experiments in this section.

Prompt Chain (PC), Chain of Thought (CoT), and Self-Consistency (SC) constitute the three core components of the prompt engineering strategy proposed in this study. To assess the individual and combined contributions of these components, we conducted an ablation experi ment evaluating GPT-4o under five distinct learning scenarios: (1) employing all three techniques (PC, CoT, and SC), (2) removing CoT, (3) removing SC, (4) removing PC, and (5) removing all three components. The results are summarized in Table 6.

The findings clearly demonstrate the necessity of integrating all three components to maximize information extraction performance. When PC, CoT, and SC were jointly applied, GPT-4o achieved the highest scores across all evaluation metrics, confirming the effectiveness of this prompt design in enhancing both accuracy and consistency. The removal of CoT resulted in a significant performance drop. In the NER task, F<sup>E</sup> fell from 0.94 to 0.77, and the RE task $P ^ { R }$ decreased from 0.90 to 0.81. This highlights the critical role of CoT in guiding the model through structured reasoning steps, particularly in tasks that involve complex inference and logical decomposition. Excluding SC also led to a marked reduction in performance. $P ^ { R }$ declined significantly to 0.84, indicating that SC helps enhance relation extraction reliability by miti gating hallucinations through iterative sampling and majority voting. This is especially important for tasks requiring multi-step validation of entity relationships. Similarly, removing PC negatively impacted model performance, reinforcing the importance of task decomposition. In the direct triple extraction setting, named entity recognition becomes an implicit process, increasing the cognitive burden on the model. By breaking down complex prompts into well-defined subproblems, PC allows the model to address each step more effectively, reducing reasoning overhead while maintaining logical consistency. When all three components were removed, overall performance deteriorated substantially. The F<sup>E</sup>dropped to 0.69, and although the decline in $P ^ { R }$ was less drastic than in the NER task, it still reached the lowest value of 0.78. In conclusion, combining PC, CoT, and SC significantly enhances LLM performance by improving reasoning depth, reducing error propagation, and promoting extraction stability. These components work synergisti cally to optimize entity recognition and relation extraction in complex KG construction tasks.

Strengthening safety awareness training for owners can create a top-down safety culture, influencing supervisors, contractors, and subcontractors.

In terms of equipment safety, failure to wear safety harnesses and helmets are the most critical risk factors, issues that have been widely discussed in existing academic research [53,54]. Regarding environ mental safety, insufficient edge protection and inadequate hole protec tion are identified as primary hazards, consistent with the existing conclusions [55,56]. These findings validate the effectiveness of the methodology proposed in this study. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on expert judgment, this research derives data-driven insights from a large dataset of historical accident reports, ensuring the robustness of its conclusions. Frequent references to safety management deficiencies and inadequate hazard detection indicate that site supervision solely reliant on designated personnel is insufficient. Once unsafe behaviors occur, they may rapidly escalate into serious accidents. Therefore, safety monitoring should be enhanced through a combination of automated equipment inspection, environmental optimization, and AI-based violation detection to interrupt accident development paths.

Additionally, since accident reports primarily document observable unsafe behaviors, this study points to positional shifts, climbing activ ities, and demolition operations as key contributing factors. In contrast, some research places greater emphasis on workers’ personal safety habits and risk perception [57,58], highlighting a difference in research focus that complements the findings of this study. By focusing on observable actions and accident status, the results of this study offer additional insights into actionable risk mitigation. Among all unsafe actions, climbing-related activities pose the highest risk. This suggests that future posture recognition systems for high-altitude operations should prioritize the detection of climbing motions to enable timely warnings and interventions. Finally, demolition work was found to carry the highest overall risk among task types, likely due to unstable struc tures and dynamic environments. Enhanced supervision and targeted protective measures are essential for workers performing demolition at heights.
6. Conclusions

This paper proposed an LLM-driven framework for automated KG construction and causal analysis of FFH accidents. By integrating a refined AcciMap-based ontology, prompt engineering strategies, and network-based topology metrics, the proposed method enables robust extraction of structured causal information from unstructured accident reports and supports comprehensive, data-driven risk factor quantitative evaluation.

This study finds the following significant findings: (1) GPT-4o ach ieved the best overall performance in both entity and relation extraction tasks, with an $F _ { 1 } ^ { E }$ of 0.94 and $P ^ { E }$ of 0.97 in NER, and a $P ^ { R }$ of 0.90 in RE. (2) The prompt design combining CP, CoT, and $\mathsf { s c }$ significantly improved model performance. Removing these components led to a drop in NER $F _ { 1 } ^ { E }$ to 0.69 and in RE $P ^ { R }$ to 0.78. (3) The proposed frame work objectively quantifies key risk factors extracted from a large number of accident reports from three perspectives. (4) Managementrelated issues, like inadequate safety management and lack of safety training, exhibit higher OD, causal proximity, and MC. Their centrality in causal pathways underscores their pivotal role in accident initiation and propagation. (5) Equipment and environment-related risks, including failure to wear harnesses and helmets and insufficient edge protection, etc., demonstrated high ID, causal proximity, and risk values, indicating they are frequent convergence points of upstream causes. (6) Observable behaviors such as unsafe climbing, demolition operations, and positional shifts showed higher risk values among all activities, offering practical insights for behavior-focused safety moni toring systems.

Despite its promising results, this paper has several limitations. First, the model may fail to identify implicit or contextually embedded en tities, especially those not explicitly stated in the text. Second, the cur rent prompt strategy adopts a fixed reasoning structure, which may limit the model’s ability to adapt to diverse accident scenarios. Third, while self-consistency improves stability, it relies on a relatively simple ma jority voting mechanism that may not fully capture nuanced causal in ferences. Future research could explore adaptive prompting strategies that include probing questions or counterfactual reasoning to enhance the extraction of implicit risk factors. Incorporating iterative voting mechanisms and expanding reasoning diversity could further reduce hallucination and improve inference accuracy. Moreover, as this paper focuses on textual data, future work could integrate computer vision techniques to link textual risk factors with observable behaviors in video data, enabling more comprehensive and real-time safety monitoring on construction sites.
